headline: Jannik Sinner wins second straight Wimbledon title after battle with Zverev
summary: The world number one secures his fifth Grand Slam title in a thrilling final on Centre Court, outlasting Alexander Zverev.
details: World number one Jannik Sinner has clinched an "amazing" fifth Grand Slam title, defeating Alexander Zverev in a hard-fought Wimbledon final on Centre Court.
Sinner overcame an early setback, dropping the first set 6-7 (7/9) before roaring back to win 7-6 (7/2), 6-3, 6-4 to secure the championship.
This victory marks Sinner's second consecutive Wimbledon title, ending a 12-month wait for a major triumph since his 2025 win at the All England Club.
The Italian star praised Zverev's performance, noting the high level of play and the intensity of the ferocious ground-strokes and thunderous serving.
Alexander Zverev, the French Open champion, will move into second place in the ATP rankings next week, posing a direct threat to Sinner's top spot.
Despite the loss, Zverev expressed pride in his first-ever Wimbledon final appearance, stating he now believes he can win the trophy in the future.

headline: Argentina coach Scaloni insists England semi-final is 'just a soccer match' despite decades of rivalry
summary: The upcoming World Cup semi-final revives one of international soccer's most storied rivalries, shaped by historical matches and political tensions like the 1982 Falklands War.
details: Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni has downplayed the historical rivalry with England ahead of their World Cup semi-final clash. He insisted the match, steeped in decades of sporting drama and political tension, is "just a soccer match. Period."

The rivalry includes England's 1966 World Cup victory, the 1982 Falklands War, and Diego Maradona's infamous "Hand of God" goal in 1986. These events have deeply shaped the narrative between the two footballing nations.

Further World Cup encounters saw Argentina advance on penalties in 1998 and England secure a 1-0 group-stage win in 2002, sending Argentina home early. These matches added layers to the intense competition.

After his side beat Switzerland 3-1 to book the clash, Scaloni reiterated his stance, stating, "Let's not look for anything else. It's a soccer match. We're going to play a soccer match against a great national team."
The Falklands (Malvinas) remain a sensitive issue, with the 1982 conflict claiming lives on both sides. The topic has resurfaced during the tournament through fan chants.
Argentina forward Jose Manuel Lopez acknowledged the "lot of history, a lot of pain" outside the pitch. However, he affirmed the players' professional approach, treating it like any other match.
Lopez emphasized that a World Cup semi-final is a dream for all players, providing ample motivation. They will leave "everything out there" on the field.
caption:
"It's a soccer match. Period. There's nothing more to it," says Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni on the upcoming World Cup semi-final against England.

Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni has downplayed the historical rivalry with England ahead of their World Cup semi-final clash. He insisted the match, steeped in decades of sporting drama and political tension, is "just a soccer match. Period."

The rivalry includes England's 1966 World Cup victory, the 1982 Falklands War, and Diego Maradona's infamous "Hand of God" goal in 1986. These events have deeply shaped the narrative between the two footballing nations.

Further World Cup encounters saw Argentina advance on penalties in 1998 and England secure a 1-0 group-stage win in 2002, sending Argentina home early. These matches added layers to the intense competition.

After his side beat Switzerland 3-1 to book the clash, Scaloni reiterated his stance, stating, "Let's not look for anything else. It's a soccer match. We're going to play a soccer match against a great national team."

The Falklands (Malvinas) remain a sensitive issue, with the 1982 conflict claiming lives on both sides. The topic has resurfaced during the tournament through fan chants.

Argentina forward Jose Manuel Lopez acknowledged the "lot of history, a lot of pain" outside the pitch. However, he affirmed the players' professional approach, treating it like any other match.

Lopez emphasized that a World Cup semi-final is a dream for all players, providing ample motivation. They will leave "everything out there" on the field.
